opus-5.5.text:
I think most people are still in the mindset that an AI model should respond instantly, because that's what we've been trained to expect from chatbots. Ask a question, get an answer in a couple of seconds. But for a lot of hard problems that isn't the right mental model. If you asked a human expert a difficult question, like proving a theorem, debugging a tricky piece of code, or working through a complicated legal or medical case, you wouldn't expect an answer in two seconds. You'd expect them to go away and think about it, maybe for hours or days.

One of the big lessons from the reasoning paradigm is that letting models think longer gives you better answers, often dramatically better, on the problems where it matters. My sense is that a lot of users haven't fully internalized that yet. They default to the fastest setting or get impatient when the model takes thirty seconds or a few minutes, and they're leaving a lot of capability on the table.

That said, it's not that every query should get maximum thinking time. If you're asking for a synonym or a quick fact, you don't need the model to deliberate for ten minutes. Part of what we have to get better at, both on the model side and the product side, is matching the amount of thinking to the difficulty of the problem, so the model knows when to answer quickly and when to dig in.

I also think expectations will shift as people see what's possible. Once you've watched a model spend a while on a problem and come back with something you couldn't have gotten otherwise, you start to appreciate that the wait was worth it. Over time I expect we'll see models thinking for much longer, hours or even days on really important problems, and people will treat that more like delegating to a colleague than querying a search engine.

r001.rationale: It describes users choosing the fastest setting and the model/product deciding how much to think based on problem difficulty, distinguishing the user’s and model’s roles.

r002.rationale: It discusses users wanting faster answers and matching thinking time to difficulty, but does not ask whether the issue is too little test-time computation or a need for models to think faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, and honestly I think most people are dramatically under-utilizing the models right now.

The way I'd frame it is that we spent years in this paradigm where the model gives you an answer in a fraction of a second, and that's just how people expect these things to work. So when you give them a model that can think for thirty seconds, or five minutes, or longer, there's this instinct to go, "That's too slow, I don't want to wait." And I understand that for a lot of queries. If you're asking what the capital of France is, you don't need the model to reason for ten minutes.

But the thing that I think people haven't fully internalized is that the value of thinking longer scales with the difficulty and the importance of the problem. If you're working on something where the answer actually matters, where a wrong answer costs you hours or days or real money, then waiting five minutes is nothing. Humans do this all the time. If you ask me a hard math question, I'm not going to answer instantly, I'm going to sit with it. And nobody considers that a failure of the human. We just accept that hard problems take time.

So when I look at how people use these models, I see a lot of situations where someone throws a genuinely hard problem at the model, gets a quick answer, and concludes the model can't do it. And often the right conclusion is that they didn't give it enough time. The capability is there, they just didn't let it use the compute.

The analogy I keep coming back to is from the poker work. When we scaled up test-time search, the amount of thinking the bot did at the table, that was worth something like a hundred thousand times the training compute in terms of performance. It was not a small effect. And I think we're in a similar place with language models, where the amount of thinking at inference time is one of the biggest levers available, and most users just have the dial turned way down.

Now, I'll say the responsibility isn't entirely on users. The models themselves should get better at knowing how long to think. You shouldn't have to decide, "Is this a thirty second problem or a thirty minute problem?" Ideally the model figures that out. And I think we'll get there. But in the meantime, my advice to people is pretty simple: when the problem is hard, let it think. You'll be surprised what comes out the other end.

r001.rationale: It says users often leave the thinking-time dial too low, while models should ideally decide how long to think.

r002.rationale: It attributes many failures to insufficient time and says models should learn to choose a thinking duration, but does not raise whether models should perform the thinking faster.

astra-6.text:
I think people are still getting used to the idea that a model might benefit from spending more time on a problem. The expectation with chatbots has been that you ask a question and get an answer almost immediately. If it takes ten seconds, that feels slow. But if you asked a colleague to solve a really difficult problem, you wouldn’t expect a good answer in ten seconds.

The right amount of time depends on what you’re asking. For a simple factual question, you want a quick response. But if you’re asking for help with a research problem or a consequential business decision, you might happily wait several minutes—or longer—if that produces a substantially better answer.

The tricky part is that waiting longer has to actually help. You need models that can use that extra computation productively, and you need some way to decide when the improvement is worth the cost. I think we’re going to move away from treating every question as deserving the same amount of effort.

r001.rationale: It says effort should vary by question and mentions deciding whether improvement justifies cost, but does not distinguish whether the model or the user determines the amount of computation.

r002.rationale: It discusses extra computation and whether it helps, but does not ask whether inadequate thinking is due to too little computation being allocated or a need for faster thinking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people are still getting used to the idea that you might want an AI to spend a long time on something. We’ve become accustomed to asking a question and getting an answer in a few seconds. And for a lot of questions, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re asking it to solve a problem that would take you several hours, it seems strange to insist that it give you an answer immediately.

The question should really be: How much is solving this problem worth to you? If it’s an important research question or a difficult programming task, you might happily wait ten minutes, or even longer, for a much better answer. You don’t necessarily need to sit there watching it. You can go do something else and come back.

Of course, the model has to earn that extra time by producing better results. But I think we’ll increasingly move toward delegating tasks, where you care more about whether the task gets done well than whether the first response arrives in two seconds.

r001.rationale: The response says users should weigh a task’s value against waiting longer, but it does not distinguish the user’s role from the model’s role in setting test-time computation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts immediate answers with waiting longer for better results, but does not frame insufficient thinking as either too little computation or a need for models to think faster.
